cover.headline: India's gold-loan leader after its windfall year: the gold price did the heavy lifting, the reset is under way, and at 1.8x forward book the stock already prices much of it
cover.lead: Muthoot Finance lends against household gold jewellery through 7,654 branches and earns returns few lenders anywhere can match (ROE 31% in FY26). But the record was made by the gold price: since FY20 the price of gold explains ~92% of the growth in its gold book; the tonnes pledged rose only 11%. In Q1FY27 the yield on loans fell from 20.8% to 17.9% as one-off recoveries ended and competition bit, and profit fell 17% from Q4. The street values the stock on **P/B (~2.0x forward book)**. We forecast EPS of ₹288.3 / ₹326.7 / ₹362.5 for FY27-29E and ROE easing from ~26% to ~22%, with the gold price held flat. Applying **1.95x to Sep-28E book of ₹1,675** (derived from its own 2.0x median since 2021 and the lender sector's move) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY.** The target needs book growth, not a re-rating. The risk is the gold price: in our bear case (gold −20%, a rate war) the stock is worth {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}; bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Gold did the lifting; Muthoot did the selling
arguments.p: Standalone gold loans grew from ₹40,700 cr (FY20) to ₹1,54,084 cr (FY26), 3.8x. The gold price rose 3.4x over the same period; the tonnes pledged only 11%; the loan-to-value of the whole book ended exactly where it started (~58% of the gold's value). In FY26 the book grew 50% while tonnes fell 6%. This is a superb business riding a commodity.

arguments.h: FY26 was the peak; FY27 is the reset
arguments.p: FY26's 20.2% standalone yield included recoveries on old bad loans, ARC receipts, auction income and top-up charges that management now calls a "windfall, onetime". Q1FY27's yield was 17.93%, NIM 10.4% (13.4% in Q4), and management guides 18-18.5% "steady state" while admitting a "determined effort to bring down the yield". We forecast EPS +{{F.epsGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27E, ahead of the street's ~5%, because the book is still growing ~5% a quarter.

arguments.h: Still the best franchise, now with company
arguments.p: Credit losses were 0.05% of loans in Q1, cost-to-income ~25%, ROA ~6%, and the new RBI gold-loan rules (in force from 1-Apr-2026) reward organised lenders. But banks hold ~₹16 lakh cr of gold loans to the NBFCs' ~₹4 lakh cr, and new entrants grew their gold books 2.5x in a year (Jefferies). We cut the yield 30bp a year from FY28.

arguments.h: Valuation: book growth, not a re-rating
arguments.p: At ₹2,737 the stock trades at 1.8x our FY28E book (median since 2021: 2.0x) and 8.4x FY28E EPS. Our {{dcf.tp|inr}} implies ~2.4x book at the target date, below today's 2.8x trailing. Cross-checks: justified P/B ₹3,229, P/E ₹2,929, residual income ₹4,216.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): management said it would revise the opening 15% AUM guidance after the half-year, and show whether the yield holds at ~18%.
The gold price: on 30-Sep-2026 22-carat gold was ~6% above end-June; every 10% move changes the value of the jewellery behind the standalone book by ~₹25,500 cr.
Competition: new entrants plan ~3,700 gold-loan branches in FY27 (Jefferies), led by Bajaj Finance; watch Muthoot's pricing and customer count.
Asset quality under the new rules: standalone Stage 2 loans rose 77% in Q1 as customers adjust to periodic interest servicing.
Credit rating: management hinted that an upgrade from AA+ is being discussed with ICRA and CRISIL; it would lower funding costs.

sections.title: One product done at scale: loans against household gold jewellery, from 5,029 branches

blocks.p: Muthoot Finance is India's largest gold-loan NBFC. A customer walks into one of its branches with household jewellery (not coins or bars), the branch tests and weighs it, and pays out a loan of up to 75-85% of its value within minutes. Most loans run 3-12 months; many customers pay the interest and principal at the end ("bullet" loans), renew, or top up when gold rises. If they do not repay, Muthoot auctions the gold, which it did for only 23,830 of ~1 crore loan accounts in FY26. Gold loans are 95% of the standalone book (₹1,63,299 cr of ₹1,72,053 cr in Jun-2026); the rest is small personal, business and property loans, mostly cross-sold to gold customers.

It earns money like any lender: it borrows at ~8.5-9% (bank loans, listed debentures, dollar bonds, commercial paper), lends at ~18% on average, and keeps the gap after branch costs (~2.3% of loans) and very small losses (0.1-0.4%). In FY26 consolidated interest income was ₹30,371 cr of ₹31,263 cr total income. Customers are small traders, farmers, self-employed and salaried households: 6.58 million active customers, average ticket ~₹1.5 lakh on new loans in FY26. The business is run by the founding family: chairman George Jacob Muthoot and MD George Alexander Muthoot lead a board with seven family executives; the promoter group owns 73.35%.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** Muthoot is the closest thing in Indian finance to a single-product utility for small borrowers who own gold. The product is simple, the collateral is liquid and the losses are tiny, so returns are high. But everything flows from one asset, the value of the jewellery: the size of the book, the yield customers will pay, the risk of losses and the competition it attracts. Subsidiaries (12% of AUM, ~10% of profit in Q1FY27) do not change that.

sections.title: From an 1887 trading house to India's largest gold lender, and one hard lesson in 2012-15

blocks.p: The Muthoot family began trading in a Kerala village in 1887 and made its first gold loan in 1939. It became an RBI-registered NBFC in 2001 and listed in 2011. The record since then has two halves. In FY13-FY15 an RBI cap on loan-to-value (60%) and a falling gold price shrank the loan book for five quarters and cut ROE from 30% to 14%. From FY20 to FY26 a rising gold price and branch growth multiplied the book nearly four times. The subsidiaries were bought or built in 2014-2016 and have added breadth but little profit until FY26.

sections.title: Gold loans: a ₹15-16 lakh crore market growing with the gold price, and suddenly crowded

blocks.p: Indian households hold about 34,600 tonnes of gold, of which only ~3,000 tonnes are pledged for loans (CRISIL, IBEF). The organised gold-loan market (banks and NBFCs) was projected at ₹15-16 lakh cr for FY26, up a third in a year (CRISIL, ICRA). Banks hold most of it (~₹16 lakh cr including farm gold loans, against ~₹4 lakh cr at NBFCs, per Muthoot's MD), often at lower rates; NBFCs win on speed, branch reach and willingness to lend without paperwork. Among NBFCs Muthoot has ~47% of the market (CRISIL, Jan-2026). About 70% of gold loans are still made in the four southern states, but growth is moving north and west.

**The competitive change of 2025-26.** For the first time, deep-pocketed AAA-rated NBFCs have entered gold lending at scale. Jefferies (10-Sep-2026) counts ₹61,900 cr of gold loans at new entrants in Jun-2026, 2.5x a year earlier and 7.6% of retail gold loans, and ~3,700 new-entrant branches planned for FY27 (vs ~1,500 in FY26), about 20% of the top four gold NBFCs' network. Bajaj Finance alone had ₹21,200 cr and targets ~₹30,000 cr by Mar-27. Muthoot's MD is dismissive ("they are not focused gold loan players ... some of them will lose interest"), but his CFO conceded on 1-Aug-2026 that a rate war is "quite possible".

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the market will keep growing as long as gold holds its value, and the new rules favour large, well-run lenders. But the economics are changing in two ways. First, competition is now coming from lenders with cheaper funding (Bajaj Finance's cost of funds was 7.4% in Q1FY27 against ~8.75% at Muthoot, per Motilal Oswal) and big balance sheets. Second, the old practice of letting interest pile up on a 12-month bullet loan, which suited customers and lenders alike, is gone: LTV now includes that interest. Both push yields down. Gold itself was ~6% above its end-June level on 30-Sep-2026, after a 15% rally in August and a 3% fall in September.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** strip out the gold price and Muthoot is a mature franchise growing in the mid-teens with falling yields. That is still a very good business (ROE in the 20s), but most of FY25-26's spectacular growth was the collateral getting more valuable, not more collateral. Our base case holds gold flat at the 30-Sep-2026 level; the bull and bear cases are, above all, gold-price cases.

sections.title: How much of the growth is the gold price? Nearly all of it, and that cuts both ways

blocks.p: A gold loan is sized by the value of the jewellery, so the book can grow in three ways: more gold pledged (tonnes), a higher gold price, or lending a larger share of the gold's value (loan-to-value, LTV). Muthoot publishes all three every quarter for the standalone book, which lets us split its growth exactly. The answer is stark. From FY20 to FY26 the gold book grew +279%; the gold price rose +240%, the tonnes pledged +11%, and the book-wide LTV ended where it began (~58% of the gold's market value, before accrued interest). On a log basis, ~92% of the growth was the price of gold.

blocks.p: **FY26 was a pure price year.** The book grew +50% although the tonnes pledged fell 6% and LTV slipped: customers who needed ₹1 lakh brought less gold because each gram was worth more ("instead of 10 grams, he needs to give only 6 grams for the same loan", MD, May-2026), and small-ticket customers left (about 15 lakh accounts below ₹30,000) while larger tickets grew. **Q1FY27 was the opposite:** the gold price fell 4% in the quarter, yet the book grew +6% because customers borrowed more against the same gold (LTV +10%), helped by the new 80-85% LTV tiers and top-ups. That pushed the book's margin of safety down to 36%, the lowest in the five quarters shown.

blocks.p: **The cushion.** In Jun-2026 the standalone book was ~64% of the value of the gold behind it (management: ~66.7% including accrued interest). A 11% fall in gold would take the average loan to 75% (the ceiling for loans above ₹5 lakh; loans above ₹3 lakh are now ~69% of the book); a 33% fall would make the average loan worth as much as its gold. New loans written at 75-85% LTV would be under water much sooner. Muthoot resets its lending rate per gram daily and holds "a cushion of at least 25% at disbursal" (AR FY2025-26), and its customers almost always repay: only 23,830 accounts went to auction in FY26 and the gold realised ₹366 cr against ₹316 cr of dues.

**The precedents.** Twice in fifteen years the gold price has turned against Muthoot. **FY13-FY15:** with an RBI cap of 60% LTV in force and gold falling, the standalone gold book shrank from ₹26,000 cr to ₹21,618 cr (−17%) in a year, tonnes from 134 to 118, profit from ₹1,004 cr to ₹671 cr and ROE from 30% to 14%. **FY21-FY23:** Muthoot's gold rate fell 12% from Sep-2020 to Mar-2021; book LTV jumped to ~75%, growth slowed to ~11% a year in FY22-23, lenders cut rates, the standalone yield fell from 20.1% (FY22) to 17.7% (FY23), Stage 3 loans rose to 4.3% (Jun-23) and group ROE fell from 28% to 18%. Losses stayed small both times. The damage was to growth, yield and ROE, not to capital.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the honest answer to "how much is gold?" is "almost everything above mid-teens growth". On 30-Sep-2026 22-carat gold was ~₹13,675 a gram in Kerala and Chennai, +6% on end-June and +2% on end-March, so the base case starts from a price close to the FY26 peak. A 20% fall would not threaten Muthoot's solvency (customers repay to get their jewellery back, and the gold would still exceed the average loan plus interest by ~17 points), but history says it would stall growth for 1-2 years and cut ROE by a third. That is the risk you take with this stock.

sections.title: The franchise: 6.6 million customers, ₹32 cr of gold loans per branch, and a shift to bigger tickets

blocks.p: Muthoot's edge is reach and habit. 5,029 standalone branches (7,654 in the group) serve ~2 lakh customers a day; 6.58 million customers had a live loan in Jun-2026. In Q1FY27 it lent ₹8,937 cr to 4.83 lakh new customers and ₹7,352 cr to 4.6 lakh returning inactive customers. Branch productivity is the profit engine: average gold loans per branch rose 40% in a year to ₹32.5 cr, almost entirely from the gold price, so each branch's fixed costs are spread over a much larger book. Cost-to-income fell from 31% (FY25) to 24% (FY26) on our basis.

blocks.p: **Bigger tickets.** The customer count has gone nowhere for a year while the book grew 44%: average loans got bigger. Management says ~15 lakh small accounts (below ₹30,000) left in FY26 and were replaced by loans of ₹50,000-2 lakh, and that loans above ₹3 lakh rose from 51% of the book in Mar-2026 to 69% in Jun-2026. Bigger tickets are cheaper to service but are exactly the customers banks and new entrants want, and they are more rate-sensitive. **Geography:** the south was 84% of the gold book in FY07 and 48% in Q1FY27; the group plans 500-600 new branches in FY27 (200-250 for Muthoot itself, ~200 gold branches at Belstar).

sections.title: The yield windfall is over: NIM fell from 13.4% to 10.4% in one quarter

blocks.p: Muthoot charges more than banks for speed and convenience: its standalone yield (interest income ÷ average loans) has ranged from 17.7% to 20.2% over FY22-26. FY26 was the top of that range, and for reasons that will not repeat. The CFO listed them on 1-Aug-2026: rising gold let customers top up and roll over loans "without needing to give any discounts", old bad loans paid in full, ARC receipts flowed to profit after the principal was recovered, auctions added income, and a rush of renewals before the new rules. The MD called FY26 "a windfall, onetime". Muthoot also raised rates by 0.5-1% on some schemes in Q4FY26. In Q1FY27 the yield fell to 17.93% and the NIM to 10.41% (13.38% in Q4). Management guides 18-18.5% "steady state".

blocks.p: **Why we expect yields to keep slipping after FY27.** Three forces push the same way. Competition: new entrants with cheaper funding are pricing to win share, and asked whether Dec-2022 to Jun-2023 (when Muthoot's yield fell ~350bp) could repeat, with every gold lender cutting rates, the CFO said "Quite possible". Mix: bigger tickets (69% of the book above ₹3 lakh) carry lower rates. Product: under the new rules interest must be serviced or counted in LTV, so the practice of letting high-rate interest accrue on old loans fades. Against that, Muthoot can reprice quickly (loans churn every ~4 months) and has "a bouquet" of schemes from 12% to 23%. We model 18.1% / 17.8% / 17.5% for FY27-29E on a consolidated basis (≈17.7-17.1% standalone). Each 10bp of yield is ~1.3% of FY28E profit.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** FY26's NIM of {{fin.nim.11|pct}} (consolidated) was a peak, and the Q1 run-rate is the better guide. We model {{F.nim.0|pct}} → {{F.nim.2|pct}} for FY27-29E. Funding will not help: the cost of borrowing rose in Q1 and the CFO expects no cut. The good news is that even at ~10.5% NIM, low costs and tiny losses still give an ROA above 5%.

sections.title: Asset quality: tiny losses on gold, a Stage 2 bump from the new rules, and Belstar's recovery

blocks.p: Gold loans rarely go bad in the way unsecured loans do: if a borrower stops paying, Muthoot sells the jewellery and usually recovers everything (FY26 auctions realised ₹366 cr against ₹316 cr of dues). Bad debts written off were 0.14% of standalone loans in FY26 and 0.05% in Q1FY27. Reported Stage 3 (non-performing) loans look high for such a safe book, 2.28% in Jun-2026, because an overdue bullet loan becomes "non-performing" even when the gold covers it: management says Stage 3 dues incl. interest were only ~58% of the gold's value in Mar-2026. From Mar-2026 the RBI asked Muthoot to classify NPAs borrower-wise rather than loan-wise, which lifted Stage 3 from 1.58% (Dec-25) to 2.35%.

blocks.p: **Two things to watch.** First, standalone Stage 2 loans jumped 77% in Q1 to ₹1,876 cr. An analyst on the call linked it to the new rules ("Stage 1, Stage 2 loans actually increased because of this regulation"): customers used to letting interest accrue for a year are being pushed to pay at least quarterly, and some fall behind on paper. If that normalises, it is noise; if not, it becomes Stage 3 and, under borrower-wise classification, drags other loans of the same customer with it. Second, **Belstar** (microfinance, 66% owned) was the source of the FY25 spike: group impairment hit ₹1,576 cr (1.5% of AUM) against ₹746 cr at the parent. Belstar's Stage 3 has since fallen from 5.5% (Mar-26) to 2.9% (Jun-26) and it earned ₹66 cr in Q1, but its book is not growing (+2% YoY).

blocks.callout: **Our forecast:** credit cost of {{F.creditCost.0|n2}}% / {{F.creditCost.1|n2}}% / {{F.creditCost.2|n2}}% of average AUM for FY27-29E, up from 0.26% in Q1 (annualised) to allow for the Stage 2 bump, a normal microfinance cycle and a less forgiving gold market. Each 10bp of credit cost is ~1.3% of FY28E profit. In the bear case (gold −20%) we add 40bp: auctions and LTV breaches rise, but history (FY14, FY23) says losses stay small; the damage is to growth and yield.

sections.title: Subsidiaries: one fast-growing gold lender, one recovering microfinance lender, and three small bets

blocks.p: The subsidiaries are 12% of group AUM and earned ~₹274 cr of the group's ₹2,825 cr profit in Q1FY27. **Muthoot Money** (100%) is the one that matters now: it pivoted from vehicle finance to gold loans in other regions and grew its book 111% to ₹10,550 cr, earning ₹172 cr in Q1 (₹338 cr in FY26 vs ₹12 cr in FY25). The parent put ₹1,000 cr of equity into it in FY26 and lends it ₹3,890 cr. **Belstar Microfinance** (66.13%) lends to women's self-help groups; after losing ₹128 cr in Q1FY26 in the industry-wide microfinance downturn it made ₹66 cr in Q1FY27, and it is opening ~200 gold-loan branches to dilute its unsecured risk. **Muthoot Homefin** (100%, affordable housing) earns a 2-7% ROE on a ₹3,496 cr book; **Asia Asset Finance** (Sri Lanka, 72.92%) and the insurance broker are small.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the subsidiaries are a sideshow to the gold book, with one exception. Muthoot Money shows how much faster a gold lender grows when it starts small (tonnes up from 7 to 12 in a year), but it also competes for the same customers in new regions. Belstar's microfinance book is a reminder that unsecured lending to the same customer segment carries real credit risk: it caused most of the group's ₹1,576 cr of FY25 impairment.

sections.title: Funding: banks, bonds and dollar notes at ~8.5-9%; short loans give a natural liquidity cushion

blocks.p: Muthoot cannot take deposits, so it borrows. In Jun-2026 the standalone company owed ₹1,49,161 cr (principal): 43% bank loans, 34% listed debentures, 17% dollar bonds (senior secured notes, hedged; ₹1,366 cr of derivative assets on the consolidated balance sheet), 4% commercial paper and ~1% other. It is rated AA+ by CRISIL and ICRA and BB+ (Fitch, S&P) / Ba1 (Moody's) abroad. Debenture funding rose 42% in Q1 alone (₹36,000 cr to ₹51,075 cr) as banks lent less. Interest cost was 7.52% of average loans in Q1 (Motilal Oswal puts the cost of borrowing at ~8.75%).

pair.title: Borrowing mix: banks 43%, debentures 34%, dollar bonds 17%
Cost of funds (our basis): ~8.8-8.9% for three years

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** NBFCs fail on liquidity before they fail on credit. Muthoot's loans are short (3-12 months) and turn over every ~4 months, while its borrowings run 1-5 years, so cash comes in faster than it goes out; it also held ₹13,419 cr of cash in Jun-2026 (9% of borrowings). The weakness is price, not access: a bank or a AAA-rated NBFC funds itself 100-150bp cheaper, which is exactly the margin new competitors are using against Muthoot.

sections.title: Capital: CRAR down from 32% to 20% as the book outgrew profit; still ample, and no raise in our model

blocks.p: Standalone capital adequacy was 20.3% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 19.39%) against the 15% minimum for NBFCs. That is well down from 31.8% in Mar-2023: the book grew 50% in FY26 and 43% in FY25 while equity grew 17% and 33% from retained profit, so the ratio fell as leverage rose. Muthoot has not raised equity since 2015; it pays a modest dividend (₹30 for FY26, 11% of EPS) and keeps the rest. Group AUM was 4.6x net worth in FY26 (3.5x in FY24).

blocks.p: **In our forecast** ROE of ~22-26% with a 12% payout grows book ~20-24% a year, faster than AUM (13-18%), so leverage falls from {{fin.leverage.11|n2}}x to {{F.leverage.2|n2}}x by FY29E and CRAR rebuilds. That is a choice, not a constraint: if gold rises again and growth returns to 30%+, CRAR would head toward the high teens and Muthoot would either slow growth, cut the dividend or raise equity. Dividends: ₹{{F.dps.0|n2}} / ₹{{F.dps.1|n2}} / ₹{{F.dps.2|n2}} for FY27-29E (yield ~{{F.divYield.0|n1}}%).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** capital is not a near-term issue: 20% CRAR on a book secured by liquid gold is strong. But the cushion has been used up quickly, and the rating agencies watch it. The payout ratio (11% in FY26 vs ~20% before) has quietly fallen to protect it; we would not expect a higher dividend while growth stays fast.

sections.title: From ROA to ROE: ~6% on assets, levered ~4.5x, gave 31% in FY26; we model ~5.5% and ~24%

blocks.p: A lender's return on equity is its return on assets times leverage. Muthoot earns an exceptional return per rupee of loans because its yield is high, its costs are spread over a very large average loan, and its losses are tiny; it needs only ~4-5x leverage (a bank runs at 10x+) to earn 20-30% on equity. The tree shows FY26's windfall and where we expect returns to settle.

sections.title: Profit doubled in FY26 on the gold price; FY27 resets to a slower, cleaner base

blocks.p: Muthoot Finance grew consolidated net profit from ₹672 cr in FY15 to ₹10,607 cr in FY26, about 28% a year, but the path was anything but smooth. Profit rose 51% in FY20 and 21% in FY21 as gold surged in the Covid years, slipped 10% in FY23 when gold went sideways and lenders cut rates, grew 20-23% in FY24-25, and then doubled (+98%) in FY26 as the gold price rose ~65% and the company collected one-off income on old loans. Q1FY27 showed the reset: profit was +43% year on year but 17% below Q4FY26 as the yield on loans fell from 20.8% to 17.9%.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** Muthoot's profit is a gold-price derivative with a very efficient machine attached. When gold rises, the same customers borrow more against the same jewellery and the machine (5,000+ branches, ~₹32 cr of gold loans per branch) turns that into profit at a 25-30% ROE. When gold stalls, growth slows and competition squeezes yields. FY26 was the best case of both. We forecast EPS growth of {{F.epsGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27E and ~11-13% a year after that, with ROE easing from {{F.roe.0|pct}} to {{F.roe.2|pct}} as yields fall.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: real in trust, reach and operations; absent in funding

blocks.p: A lender's moat shows up as a lasting gap between what it earns on loans and what it pays for money, costs and losses. Muthoot's standalone ROA has been 5.7-7.6% of loans every year since FY22, two to three times a typical Indian NBFC. We test where that edge comes from and whether new competitors can copy it.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Muthoot has a genuine operating moat: trust, reach and a process for handling gold at scale that took decades to build. That moat protects its volumes and its losses. It does not protect its price. When better-funded lenders decide gold loans are worth fighting for, as they did in FY23 and again now, Muthoot keeps its customers by cutting rates. The moat supports a 20%+ ROE, not a 30% one.

blocks.p: Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) split the market. sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books, lumpy income and thin disclosure on yields

blocks.p: We rate accounting **AMBER**. The joint auditors (Krishnamoorthy & Krishnamoorthy and PSDY & Associates) reported no qualification on FY26, the company holds ₹295 cr of provisions above its expected-loss model, and Muthoot discloses tonnes, gold price and margin of safety every quarter, which few lenders would. But four things deserve a reader's attention:

bullets: **Lumpy, undisclosed one-offs in interest income.** FY26 included ~₹500 cr of interest written back on recovered bad loans (Q3, per an analyst on the Q4 call), ~₹85 cr of auction and ARC income in Q4 and top-up charges. Management will not split clean and one-off yield ("we don't have any bifurcation"), so the quality of any quarter's margin is hard to judge.

**Accrued interest on bullet loans.** Interest on a 12-month bullet loan is booked as it accrues but collected at maturity, so profit runs ahead of cash. The new RBI rules (interest counted in LTV; renewal only after paying interest) reduce this; Stage 2 rose as customers adjusted.

**Classification changes.** From Mar-2026 NPAs are classified borrower-wise at the RBI's advice, so Stage 3 history is not like-for-like (1.58% Dec-25 → 2.35% Mar-26). FY25 impairment was restated from ₹1,635 cr to ₹1,576 cr in the FY26 accounts.

**Related parties.** The parent lends ₹3,890 cr to Muthoot Money; some branch and office premises were acquired from or are linked to promoter-family members (AR title-deed schedule); seven family members draw executive pay (see governance).

sections.title: Ownership: the Muthoot family owns 73%, domestic funds are buying

blocks.p: In Jun-2026 the Muthoot family (promoter group) held 73.35%, unchanged for years and with nothing pledged. The holdings are spread across the second and third generations: chairman George Jacob Muthoot and George Thomas Muthoot 10.87% each, MD George Alexander Muthoot 5.89%, and family members 3.7-7.5% each. The free float is only ~27%. Foreign investors held 11.61% (12.31% in Mar-2026) and mutual funds 9.51%, led by SBI Mutual Fund (5.35%). Retail holders own 4.29%.

sections.title: Management and governance: family-run, conservative with the balance sheet, generous with its own pay

blocks.p: Muthoot is run by the family that founded it. George Jacob Muthoot is chairman and George Alexander Muthoot managing director; George Thomas Muthoot (joint MD) and four other family members are whole-time directors, including three of the next generation. Eight independent directors sat on the board in Jun-2026. The company is an RBI "upper layer" NBFC with bank-like governance rules. Joint auditors Krishnamoorthy & Krishnamoorthy and PSDY & Associates (appointed to 2027) reported no qualification on FY26.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a BUY on the street's yardstick, and a bet that gold holds its value

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest and most efficient gold lender: 5,029 branches, 6.6 million active customers, credit losses of 0.05-0.15% a year, cost-to-income ~25%, an ROE of 18-31% in every year since FY20, a 73% family owner that has not diluted shareholders since 2015, and a balance sheet secured by the most liquid collateral a household owns. What you are also buying is a gold-price derivative: ~92% of the growth in its gold book since FY20 came from the price of gold.

**What you are paying:** 1.8x our FY28E book and 8.4x FY28E EPS, below the stock's 2.0x median forward P/B since 2021, after a 34% fall from January. Our 1.95x on Sep-28E book gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}) and a BUY; the target implies ~2.4x book at the target date, below today's 2.8x trailing, so it needs book growth (~20%+ a year), not a re-rating. The market price implies a long-run ROE of only ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}}: it is already discounting part of a gold or competition shock.

**On today's numbers we would stay buyers below ~₹2,840 and turn sellers above ~₹3,440.** The rating is close to the line: at 1.8x Sep-28E book the target is ~₹3,020 (HOLD); at 2.1x (Jefferies' reference multiple) ~₹3,520.

**Biggest swing factors:** the gold price (it sets AUM growth and the multiple), the yield (10bp ≈ 1.3% of FY28E EPS) and the multiple (0.25x ≈ ₹419 a share). A 20% fall in gold would still leave a ~17-point cushion between the average loan (incl. interest) and its gold, so this is an earnings and multiple risk, not a solvency risk.

**Portfolio fit:** a high-return, low-multiple financial that doubles as a hedge-like exposure to the gold price. Size the position for the bear case ({{scen.bear.tp|inr}}), and treat gold-price weakness as the signal to reassess, not the Q2 headline.
